introLesson.title: Introduction to Macbeth

sections.authorBiography: William Shakespeare was baptized in Stratford-upon-Avon on 26 April 1564, the son of John Shakespeare, a glover and town official, and Mary Arden. He probably attended Stratford's grammar school, married Anne Hathaway in 1582, and had three children: Susanna and the twins Hamnet and Judith (Hamnet died aged eleven in 1596). By the early 1590s he was an actor and playwright in London; from 1594 he was a sharer in the Lord Chamberlain's Men, who built the Globe theatre in 1599 and became the King's Men when James VI of Scotland became James I of England in 1603. He wrote or co-wrote about 38 plays and the Sonnets, and died in Stratford on 23 April 1616. Seven years later his fellow actors John Heminges and Henry Condell published 36 of his plays in the First Folio (1623).
sections.historicalContext: Macbeth was written around 1606 for a company that now served a Scottish king. James I was fascinated by witchcraft (he wrote a treatise, Daemonologie, in 1597, and had taken part in witch trials in Scotland) and traced his descent from Banquo, whom the play makes noble. In November 1605 the Gunpowder Plot to blow up the king and Parliament was discovered; at the 1606 trial of the Jesuit Henry Garnet, "equivocation" (misleading by ambiguous speech) became notorious, and the Porter's joke about an "equivocator" in Act II, Scene III points to it. Shakespeare took his story from Raphael Holinshed's Chronicles (1587), changing much: the historical Macbeth ruled Scotland from 1040 to 1057 and killed Duncan I in battle, not in his bed.

publicationAndReception.publication: The play was first printed in the First Folio (1623), the only early text. It is Shakespeare's shortest tragedy, and most scholars think the version we have was adapted after his death, with the Hecate passages probably added by Thomas Middleton. The earliest surviving eyewitness account of a performance is the astrologer Simon Forman's description of a Macbeth at the Globe in April 1611.
publicationAndReception.then: Little is recorded about first reactions. After the theatres reopened in 1660, William Davenant staged a version with added songs and flying witches that held the stage for decades; the actor David Garrick restored much of Shakespeare's text in 1744. Romantic critics such as Thomas De Quincey ("On the Knocking at the Gate in Macbeth," 1823) praised its psychological intensity.
publicationAndReception.now: Macbeth is among the most performed and taught of all plays. Film versions range from Akira Kurosawa's Throne of Blood (1957) to Roman Polanski's (1971) and Joel Coen's The Tragedy of Macbeth (2021). Theatre superstition calls it "the Scottish play" and avoids saying its name backstage. Modern critics debate its gender politics (Lady Macbeth's "unsex me here"), its view of fate and free will, and its politics of tyranny and succession.

sections.overview: Returning from a victorious battle, the Scottish general Macbeth meets three witches who greet him with titles, including "king hereafter." What Macbeth and his wife do with that prophecy, and what it does to them and to Scotland, is the play.

sections.whyItMatters: Macbeth is the classic study of how a decent, admired person talks himself into doing evil, and of how leaders who seize power must keep using violence to hold it. Those patterns are visible in politics and in ordinary life, and the play's language about guilt has entered everyday English ("out, damned spot").

spoilerOverview.text: Macbeth murders King Duncan in his sleep, urged by Lady Macbeth; Duncan's sons flee and Macbeth is crowned. He has Banquo murdered (Fleance escapes), sees Banquo's ghost, returns to the witches and receives riddling prophecies, and has Macduff's family slaughtered. Lady Macbeth sleepwalks and dies, probably by suicide. Malcolm's army, carrying branches from Birnam Wood, attacks Dunsinane; Macduff, "from his mother's womb / Untimely ripp'd," kills Macbeth, and Malcolm becomes king.

passage.quote: Fair is foul, and foul is fair
passage.use: The witches' chant in the first scene: the play's motto. Values are inverted and appearances lie.

The Middleton revision of the Hecate scenes is the majority view, not a certainty.
Whether Lady Macbeth's death is suicide rests on Malcolm's report in the last scene ("by self and violent hands"); present it as reported.

segments.phase: I do: the book in one passage
segments.activity: Model a close reading of one passage using the written think-aloud below.
segments.script: First, meaning. I read “Fair is foul, and foul is fair” slowly and put it in my own words: The three witches chant together that fair is foul and foul is fair. Next, craft. I notice the chiasmus, a mirrored pattern that flips good and bad in a single line, like a spell. The strongest word is “foul”: the word for ugly or evil is set equal to "fair," so values are turned upside down. Then, effect. What does the witches' chant tell us about the world of the play? My answer: The witches announce a world where appearances deceive and moral order is reversed; Macbeth, who seems a loyal hero, will become a murderer, and his first line will echo theirs.

segments.activity: Read the spoiler-free overview together and name the themes to track.
segments.script: What the book is about (no spoilers): Returning from a victorious battle, the Scottish general Macbeth meets three witches who greet him with titles, including "king hereafter." What Macbeth and his wife do with that prophecy, and what it does to them and to Scotland, is the play. Themes to track: ambition: watch how wanting becomes doing, and what each crime demands next. fate and free will: the witches predict, but who decides? appearance and reality: "fair is foul": faces, words and prophecies that hide their meaning. guilt and conscience: blood, sleep and hands; how guilt shows itself. masculinity and power: what "being a man" means to each character.

segments.activity: Exit ticket on the author and context (answer given).
segments.script: Shakespeare wrote Macbeth around 1606, soon after King James I, who believed in witchcraft and claimed descent from Banquo, survived the Gunpowder Plot to blow up Parliament. How might that context shape a play about killing a king? Answer: Accept answers such as: James's interest in witches explains their prominence; showing regicide as monstrous flattered a king who had just escaped assassination; Banquo is shown as noble because he was James's ancestor.

lessonPlan.title: Macbeth unit
lessonPlan.author: William Shakespeare
lessonPlan.edition: First Folio (1623) text as edited by Standard Ebooks
lessonPlan.editionNote: Macbeth survives only in the 1623 First Folio. The reading text is the Standard Ebooks edition, divided into the conventional 28 scenes (plus the cast list). Most scholars think the Hecate passages (Act III, Scene V and part of Act IV, Scene I) were added by another writer, probably Thomas Middleton. Cite act, scene and line from this edition.
lessonPlan.gradeBand: Grades 9–12 (scales to graduate via rigor levels)

strategies.label: Wait time
strategies.howTo: Pause at least 3 seconds after asking (5 to 10 for DOK 3 and 4 questions) before calling on anyone, and pause again after a student answers so others can add on. Call on students at random, not only volunteers.

strategies.label: Think-pair-share
strategies.howTo: One minute of silent thinking or jotting, two minutes with a partner, then pairs report. Use it for every DOK 3 and 4 question so all students rehearse an answer.

strategies.label: Follow-up probes
strategies.howTo: Answer a response with a probe instead of a verdict: ask for the line that proves it, ask "why?" or "how do you know?", or ask another student to agree, extend or challenge.

strategies.label: Student-generated questions
strategies.howTo: Students write their own questions at each level (a recall, a "why/how" and a "should/what if" question), trade them, and answer a classmate's. The teacher picks one or two for the whole class.

strategies.label: Turn and talk
strategies.howTo: A 60-second partner check for literal questions, so every student says the answer aloud before one is called on.

strategies.label: Cold call with support
strategies.howTo: Call on a student by name after the wait time; if they are stuck, offer a choice of two answers or let them "phone a friend" and come back to them.

strategies.label: Socratic circle
strategies.howTo: Inner circle discusses for 5 minutes while the outer circle tracks evidence and questions; then swap.

strategies.label: Four corners / take a stand
strategies.howTo: Students move to Agree / Somewhat agree / Somewhat disagree / Disagree and must cite a line to defend the position; anyone may move after hearing evidence.

literal.label: Literal / recall
literal.scaffold: Sentence starter: “In this scene, … because the text says …”
literal.extension: Note how this detail is set up or echoed elsewhere in Macbeth.
followUps: Where exactly does it say that? Read us the line.
Who can add a detail that comes just before or after?

inferential.label: Inferential / analytical
inferential.scaffold: Sentence starter: “The text says …, which suggests … because …”
inferential.extension: Test your reading against one critical approach (formalist, historicist, psychoanalytic, feminist) and say what it adds.
followUps: What in the text makes you think so?
Does anyone read that line differently? What would change?

evaluative.label: Evaluative / synthesis / creative
evaluative.scaffold: Sentence starter: “I (dis)agree that … because …; someone might object that …, but …”
evaluative.extension: Situate your judgment in a critical conversation about Macbeth: whose reading does yours support or challenge?
followUps: What is the strongest argument against your position?
What evidence would make you change your mind?

middleSchool.note: Excerpt-based: read the passage aloud first; use the scaffolds; accept partial answers and build with probes.

hsFreshman.note: Use the scaffolds for literal and inferential items; require one quotation for every inferential answer.

hsSophomore.note: Require a quotation and an explanation; push evaluative answers to address a counterclaim.

hsJunior.note: Emphasize structure and ambiguity; students should name where the text leaves matters open.

hsSenior.note: Weigh competing interpretations; students should defend the stronger reading.

ap.note: Treat each evaluative item as a thesis rehearsal: defensible claim, purposeful evidence, commentary on choices.

collegeFreshman.note: Add the extension: connect answers to historical context and one secondary perspective.

collegeSophomore.note: Use the extensions: genre and period conventions, and a published critic.

collegeJunior.note: Use the extensions: name a critical method and test it against the passage.

collegeSenior.note: Use the extensions: connect the scene to the whole work and the scholarship.

graduate.note: Use the extensions: position answers in a critical conversation and the textual history.

questioning.alignment: Questioning design (our description; see docs/questioning-alignment.md): every lesson offers questions at three cognitive levels with DOK tags, built-in wait time, follow-up probes after each answer, think-pair-share for higher-order items and a student-generated question routine, with a level-specific focus set for each of the eleven rigor levels. It is designed to support classroom observation frameworks such as the NIET Teaching Standards Rubric (Questioning indicator); it is not NIET material and is not endorsed by NIET.

lessonPlan.middleSchoolTrack: Scaffolded-support track (grade-9 floor): students work from teacher-selected passages with scaffolds, sentence starters and partial-credit probes.

segments.activity: Students write to the bell-ringer, then pair-share.
segments.script: Project the day's bell-ringer question (each lesson of Macbeth has its own). Students write silently for 5 minutes, then pair-share for 3. Call on one volunteer and one non-volunteer, and connect their answers to ambition and its costs.

segments.activity: The day's key words in context, with verified word histories.
segments.script: Introduce the day's words in the sentences where they appear in Macbeth. Read each sentence aloud, ask students to guess the meaning from context, then give the gloss and the word history. Students copy one word into their journal with their own sentence.

Give the 10-minute background talk from the day's lesson: what happens in this scene, the context a reader needs, and the literary elements to watch. Pause once to ask a check-for-understanding question.

segments.activity: Model the close reading of the anchor quotation using the written think-aloud in the day's lesson.
segments.script: Read the anchor passage aloud twice. Model the three steps out loud: what the words say, what craft choice stands out and why, and what effect it has on the reader. The day's lesson gives the passage and a full written think-aloud.

segments.activity: Guided analysis of a second quotation; expected answers given.
segments.script: Display the second passage. Students annotate it in pairs using the same three steps; circulate, then take answers to the two guided questions and confirm them against the expected answers in the day's lesson.

segments.activity: Independent annotation and a claim-evidence-reasoning paragraph (exemplar given).
segments.script: Students annotate the scene on their own (three marks with a margin note each) and write one claim-evidence-reasoning paragraph on the day's focus, then begin the writing prompt at their assigned rigor level.

segments.activity: Structured discussion from the 30 tiered questions, with facilitation notes.
segments.script: Run a 10-minute discussion from the day's anchor question and tiered questions. Start with literal checks, move to inference, and end with one evaluative question that ties the scene to ambition and its costs.

segments.activity: Scene quiz in the app and an exit ticket (answer given).
segments.script: Students take the scene quiz in the app, then answer the one-sentence exit ticket with a short quotation. Collect the tickets to plan the next lesson.

segments.activity: Summarize the lesson and preview the next reading.
segments.script: Restate the day's takeaway in one sentence, ask two students to name the line that best proves it, and preview the next reading in Macbeth.

objectives: Students will cite at least 2 quotations, with locations, to support each written claim about what the text says explicitly and implicitly (scored on the writing-prompt rubric).
Students will trace one theme across at least 3 sections of the play in the final paper, earning at least 70 of 100 rubric points.
Students will explain how characters, setting and point of view interact in at least 3 exit tickets, each meeting the claim-evidence-reasoning criteria.
Students will determine the in-context meaning of taught vocabulary, scoring at least 80% on the vocabulary items of the scene quizzes.
Students will write an argument with a clear claim, reasons and relevant evidence, scoring at least 80% on the unit test's short-answer scoring guides.

wholeBookTest.title: Macbeth: unit test

items.prompt: What voice does Macbeth say he heard?
options: Sleep no more! Macbeth does murder sleep

items.prompt: What word could Macbeth not say?
In the line “Had he not resembled My father as he slept, I had done’t.”, what does “resembled” most nearly mean?

In the line “But I remember now I am in this earthly world; where to do harm Is often laudable, to do good sometime Accounted dangerous folly: why then, alas, Do I put up that womanly defence, To say I have done no harm?”, what does “laudable” most nearly mean?
Who warns her to flee?
Who visits her and then leaves?
What does she tell her son about his father?
options: That he is dead and a traitor

items.prompt: What does Macduff reveal about his birth?
options: He was untimely ripped from his mother's womb

items.prompt: What does Macduff bring on stage?
What new title does Malcolm give the thanes?
What does this passage most clearly show? “Three Witches” (Dramatis Personae)

Hyperbole of guilt. The words “Will all great Neptune’s ocean wash this blood / Clean from my hand” (Act II, Scene II, Macbeth) are the evidence: their wording makes this point in the text itself.
Lady Macduff on Macduff's flight.

The son's wit. The words “Then the liars and swearers are fools, for there are liars and swearers enow to beat the honest men and hang up them” (Act IV, Scene II, Son) are the evidence: their wording makes this point in the text itself.
His response. The words “She should have died hereafter” (Act V, Scene V, Macbeth) are the evidence: their wording makes this point in the text itself.

Bear-baiting image. The words “They have tied me to a stake; I cannot fly, / But, bear-like, I must fight the course” (Act V, Scene VII, Macbeth) are the evidence: their wording makes this point in the text itself.

Both are listed as "general of the king's army," so when the witches speak to both, the difference in what they do will come from character, not position. The words “Macbeth, general of the king’s army” (Dramatis Personae) are the evidence: their wording makes this point in the text itself. This develops masculinity and power: almost all named roles are men defined by military or noble rank; the three women with lines are Lady Macbeth, Lady Macduff and the Gentlewoman, plus Hecate and the Witches, whose power is outside the social order.
Setting

Her resolve. The words “We fail! / But screw your courage to the sticking-place, / And we’ll not fail” (Act I, Scene VII, Lady Macbeth) are the evidence: their wording makes this point in the text itself. This develops masculinity and power: she defines manhood as the will to murder.
Act II, Scene I

He calls it "a dagger of the mind, a false creation, / Proceeding from the heat-oppressed brain," knowing his imagination is creating the weapon, yet he follows it: "I go, and it is done.". The words “A dagger of the mind, a false creation, / Proceeding from the heat-oppressed brain” (Act II, Scene I, Macbeth) are the evidence: their wording makes this point in the text itself. This develops guilt and conscience: guilt begins before the deed; his mind projects the act.

Decision. The words “I go, and it is done; the bell invites me” (Act II, Scene I, Macbeth) are the evidence: their wording makes this point in the text itself. This develops guilt and conscience: guilt begins before the deed; his mind projects the act.

She says "security / Is mortals' chiefest enemy" and that Macbeth will "spurn fate, scorn death.". The words “He shall spurn fate, scorn death, and bear” (Act III, Scene V, Hecate) are the evidence: their wording makes this point in the text itself. This develops fate and free will: Hecate says security is "mortals' chiefest enemy.".
Act III, Scene V

He says "the gracious Duncan / Was pitied of Macbeth: marry, he was dead," a joke that accuses. The words “The gracious Duncan / Was pitied of Macbeth: marry, he was dead” (Act III, Scene VI, Lennox) are the evidence: their wording makes this point in the text itself. This develops appearance and reality: speech must be guarded under tyranny.

Scotland under tyranny. The words “this our suffering country / Under a hand accursed” (Act III, Scene VI, Lennox) are the evidence: their wording makes this point in the text itself. This develops appearance and reality: speech must be guarded under tyranny.
Act IV, Scene I
Dramatic irony

Guilt. The words “Now does he feel / His secret murders sticking on his hands” (Act V, Scene II, Angus) are the evidence: their wording makes this point in the text itself. This develops ambition: the stolen title does not fit.

Angus says his title hangs "like a giant's robe / Upon a dwarfish thief," and his soldiers "move only in command, / Nothing in love.". The words “Those he commands move only in command, / Nothing in love” (Act V, Scene II, Angus) are the evidence: their wording makes this point in the text itself. This develops ambition: the stolen title does not fit.

Macbeth's "confidence" (the security Hecate promised) keeps him behind his walls. The words “the confident tyrant / Keeps still in Dunsinane” (Act V, Scene IV, Siward) are the evidence: their wording makes this point in the text itself. This develops fate and free will: prophecy fulfilled through practical choices.

Meaninglessness. The words “it is a tale / Told by an idiot, full of sound and fury, / Signifying nothing” (Act V, Scene V, Macbeth) are the evidence: their wording makes this point in the text itself. This develops fate and free will: meaninglessness.
Act V, Scene VIII

Malcolm calls him "this dead butcher," but his last words, "Lay on, Macduff," show courage. The words “Lay on, Macduff, / And damn’d be him that first cries, “Hold, enough” (Act V, Scene VIII, Macbeth) are the evidence: their wording makes this point in the text itself. This develops fate and free will: the equivocal prophecy completed.

The identical title makes Banquo Macbeth's double and foil. The words “Banquo, general of the king’s army” (Dramatis Personae) are the evidence: their wording makes this point in the text itself. This develops masculinity and power: almost all named roles are men defined by military or noble rank; the three women with lines are Lady Macbeth, Lady Macduff and the Gentlewoman, plus Hecate and the Witches, whose power is outside the social order. Both are listed as "general of the king's army," so when the witches speak to both, the difference in what they do will come from character, not position.

Paradox: every battle is lost by someone. The words “When the hurlyburly’s done, / When the battle’s lost and won” (Act I, Scene I, Second Witch) are the evidence: their wording makes this point in the text itself. This develops appearance and reality: the first scene announces that nothing will be what it seems. The witches' chant "Fair is foul, and foul is fair" collapses good and evil into each other, and their paradox "the battle's lost and won" warns that victory and defeat can be the same event.

The play's first description of Macbeth: heroic. The words “For brave Macbeth—well he deserves that name” (Act I, Scene II, Sergeant) are the evidence: their wording makes this point in the text itself. This develops ambition: Macbeth's violence is first shown as loyalty; the same violence will serve ambition. The Captain calls him "brave Macbeth" who "unseam'd" the rebel "from the nave to the chaps," and Duncan's "What he hath lost noble Macbeth hath won" echoes the witches, binding Macbeth to Cawdor's treachery.

Graphic violence praised as service. The words “Till he unseam’d him from the nave to the chaps” (Act I, Scene II, Sergeant) are the evidence: their wording makes this point in the text itself. This develops ambition: Macbeth's violence is first shown as loyalty; the same violence will serve ambition. The Captain calls him "brave Macbeth" who "unseam'd" the rebel "from the nave to the chaps," and Duncan's "What he hath lost noble Macbeth hath won" echoes the witches, binding Macbeth to Cawdor's treachery.

Banquo's warning. The words “oftentimes, to win us to our harm, / The instruments of darkness tell us truths” (Act I, Scene III, Banquo) are the evidence: their wording makes this point in the text itself. This develops fate and free will: the prophecy makes no demand; Macbeth's "horrible imaginings" supply the murder. Banquo warns that "the instruments of darkness tell us truths" to win us "to our harm," while Macbeth asks why he yields "to that suggestion / Whose horrid image doth unfix my hair": the "suggestion" of murder comes from within.

Darkness by day. The words “by the clock, ’tis day, / And yet dark night strangles the travelling lamp” (Act II, Scene IV, Ross) are the evidence: their wording makes this point in the text itself. This develops fate and free will: the cosmic order reacts to a human crime. Ross sees that "dark night strangles the travelling lamp" by day, and a falcon is killed by "a mousing owl," a lower creature overthrowing a higher, just as Macbeth killed his king.

Symbol of regicide. The words “A falcon, towering in her pride of place, / Was by a mousing owl hawk’d at and kill’d” (Act II, Scene IV, Old Man) are the evidence: their wording makes this point in the text itself. This develops fate and free will: the cosmic order reacts to a human crime. Ross sees that "dark night strangles the travelling lamp" by day, and a falcon is killed by "a mousing owl," a lower creature overthrowing a higher, just as Macbeth killed his king.

Childlessness. The words “Upon my head they placed a fruitless crown, / And put a barren sceptre in my gripe” (Act III, Scene I, Macbeth) are the evidence: their wording makes this point in the text itself. This develops ambition: ambition fulfilled breeds insecurity and more crime. He says "To be thus is nothing; / But to be safely thus," and sees his "fruitless crown" passing to Banquo's line.

Torment. The words “O, full of scorpions is my mind, dear wife” (Act III, Scene II, Macbeth) are the evidence: their wording makes this point in the text itself. This develops guilt and conscience: both are unhappy: "Nought's had, all's spent.". She admits "Nought's had, all's spent, / Where our desire is got without content," and he keeps her "innocent of the knowledge" of Banquo's murder.

Guilt made visible; Macbeth resolves to wade on. The words “Act III, Scene IV” (Act III, Scene IV, Macbeth) are the evidence: their wording makes this point in the text itself. This develops guilt and conscience: guilt made visible; Macbeth resolves to wade on. He tells the ghost "never shake / Thy gory locks at me," and afterward says he is "in blood / Stepp'd in so far" that turning back would be as hard as going on.

Hecate's complaint. The words “Saucy and overbold” (Act III, Scene V, Hecate) are the evidence: their wording makes this point in the text itself. This develops fate and free will: Hecate says security is "mortals' chiefest enemy.". She says "security / Is mortals' chiefest enemy" and that Macbeth will "spurn fate, scorn death.".

Echoes Macbeth's ocean. The words “Here’s the smell of the blood still: all the perfumes of Arabia will not sweeten this little hand” (Act V, Scene I, Lady Macbeth) are the evidence: their wording makes this point in the text itself. This develops guilt and conscience: what she suppressed now speaks. She once said "A little water clears us of this deed," but now cries "all the perfumes of Arabia will not sweeten this little hand.".

Guilt as stain. The words “Out, damned spot! out, I say” (Act V, Scene I, Lady Macbeth) are the evidence: their wording makes this point in the text itself. This develops guilt and conscience: what she suppressed now speaks. She once said "A little water clears us of this deed," but now cries "all the perfumes of Arabia will not sweeten this little hand.".

Clothing imagery. The words “now does he feel his title / Hang loose about him, like a giant’s robe / Upon a dwarfish thief” (Act V, Scene II, Angus) are the evidence: their wording makes this point in the text itself. This develops ambition: the stolen title does not fit. Angus says his title hangs "like a giant's robe / Upon a dwarfish thief," and his soldiers "move only in command, / Nothing in love.".

Autumn imagery. The words “I have lived long enough: my way of life / Is fall’n into the sear, the yellow leaf” (Act V, Scene III, Macbeth) are the evidence: their wording makes this point in the text itself. This develops guilt and conscience: he asks the Doctor to "minister to a mind diseased.". He says his life "is fall'n into the sear, the yellow leaf," and asks the Doctor to "minister to a mind diseased.".

Malcolm's order. The words “Let every soldier hew him down a bough / And bear’t before him” (Act V, Scene IV, Malcolm) are the evidence: their wording makes this point in the text itself. This develops fate and free will: prophecy fulfilled through practical choices. Malcolm orders "every soldier hew him down a bough," to "shadow / The numbers of our host.".

The strategy. The words “thereby shall we shadow / The numbers of our host” (Act V, Scene IV, Malcolm) are the evidence: their wording makes this point in the text itself. This develops fate and free will: prophecy fulfilled through practical choices. Malcolm orders "every soldier hew him down a bough," to "shadow / The numbers of our host.".

Prophecy fulfilled through practical choices: malcolm's order. The words “Act V, Scene IV” (Act V, Scene IV, Malcolm) are the evidence: their wording makes this point in the text itself. This develops fate and free will: prophecy fulfilled through practical choices. Malcolm orders "every soldier hew him down a bough," to "shadow / The numbers of our host.".

Time. The words “To-morrow, and to-morrow, and to-morrow, / Creeps in this petty pace from day to day” (Act V, Scene V, Macbeth) are the evidence: their wording makes this point in the text itself. This develops fate and free will: meaninglessness. Life is "a tale / Told by an idiot, full of sound and fury, / Signifying nothing.".

Battle. The words “Make all our trumpets speak” (Act V, Scene VI, Macduff) are the evidence: their wording makes this point in the text itself. This develops fate and free will: the prophecy is fulfilled. Malcolm orders "your leavy screens throw down" and the trumpets become "harbingers of blood and death.".

Malcolm's command. The words “your leavy screens throw down” (Act V, Scene VI, Malcolm) are the evidence: their wording makes this point in the text itself. This develops fate and free will: the prophecy is fulfilled. Malcolm orders "your leavy screens throw down" and the trumpets become "harbingers of blood and death.".

False security: bear-baiting image. The words “Act V, Scene VII” (Act V, Scene VII, Macbeth) are the evidence: their wording makes this point in the text itself. This develops fate and free will: false security. He is "tied ... to a stake" like a bear but trusts that his enemies are "born of woman.".

Macbeth's confidence. The words “Thou wast born of woman” (Act V, Scene VII, Macbeth) are the evidence: their wording makes this point in the text itself. This develops fate and free will: false security. He is "tied ... to a stake" like a bear but trusts that his enemies are "born of woman.".

prompts.text: Analyze how William Shakespeare develops ambition and its costs across Macbeth. Trace the idea through at least three moments (beginning, middle and end) and argue what the ending finally suggests.
Choose one recurring symbol, image or motif in Macbeth and argue how its meaning changes over the play and why that change matters to fate and free will.
Analyze a central character's choices in Macbeth. Argue whether the play judges that character, and how its structure or point of view shapes your answer.
Two readers disagree about whether Macbeth finally endorses or criticizes its society's view of guilt and conscience. Weigh both readings and argue for one, answering the strongest objection.

evidence.sections: at least three sections, from the beginning, middle and end
evidence.citation: Quote the reading text exactly and cite the act, scene and line (MLA style).
evidence.outsideSources: HS Senior and above: one scholarly or historical source; College Sophomore and above: two, cited in MLA.

rubric.descriptor: A specific, arguable claim that answers the prompt and organizes the paper.
Well-chosen, accurately quoted and cited passages from across the work, meeting the evidence requirement.
Explains how language, structure and literary elements create meaning; goes beyond summary.
Logical progression, clear topic sentences and transitions; introduction and conclusion frame the argument.
Formal academic voice, present tense for literature, correct grammar and MLA format.
